label: Bonus Class 2
title: Consonant Clusters: Why We Say "Isport"
bigIdea: English words can start with two or three consonant sounds together (black, please, school). Standard Arabic words never start that way, so our mouth adds a sneaky vowel (bilack, pilease, iskool). A detective catches the sneaky vowel and glues the sounds together.
bigIdeaAr: يمكن أن تبدأ الكلمة الإنجليزية بصوتين صامتين أو ثلاثة معاً (black و please و school)، أما الكلمة العربية الفصيحة فلا تبدأ هكذا أبداً، لذلك يضيف فمنا حركة متسللة (بِلاك، بِليز، إسكول). المحقق يمسك الحركة المتسللة ويلصق الصوتين معاً.
builtOn: Lessons 5-8: my/your, have got (glasses, phone), body (eyebrow), My Classroom (classroom, playground, student)
Phonics Lesson 5: th and ng (thin, this, ring, king)
Phonics Lesson 7: L-blends bl, cl, fl, pl, sl (black, clap, flag, plum, slide)
Bonus Class 1: a digraph is two letters for ONE sound
Preview only (taught later): R-blends in Lesson 9 and S-blends in Lesson 11

objectives.en: I can explain the difference between a digraph (sh = one sound) and a cluster (bl = two sounds).
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أفرّق بين الحرف المزدوج (sh صوت واحد) وتجمّع الصوامت (bl صوتان).

objectives.en: I can say why Arabic speakers add a vowel (bilack, isport).
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أشرح لماذا يضيف متحدثو العربية حركة (بِلاك، إسبورت).

objectives.en: I can say black, please, flag and student without a sneaky vowel.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أنطق black و please و flag و student بدون حركة متسللة.

objectives.en: I can say ng as one sound at the end of king and ring.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أنطق ng صوتاً واحداً في آخر king و ring.

keyTerms.meaning: Two or three consonant sounds side by side, and you can hear each one: b-l in black.
Two letters, ONE sound: sh in fish (from Bonus Class 1).
One beat of a word. Each beat has one vowel sound: black = 1 beat.
An extra vowel our mouth adds by mistake: bi-lack, i-sport.
One nose sound at the end of king, ring, sing. No hard g after it.

facts.en: Every language has rules for how a syllable may start. In Standard Arabic, a syllable always starts with one consonant and then a vowel: ka-ta-ba. Two consonants at the very start are not allowed.
facts.ar: لكل لغة قوانين لبداية المقطع. في العربية الفصحى يبدأ المقطع دائماً بصوت صامت واحد ثم حركة: كَـ تَـ بَ. ولا يُسمح بصوتين صامتين في البداية.

facts.en: Arabic solves this with hamzat al-wasl. Words like اسْم and اسْتَمَعَ begin with a letter that has sukun, so when you START with them you add a helping hamza with a vowel: 'ism', 'istama'a'. In the middle of a sentence the helper disappears: وَاسْتَمَعَ is said 'wa-stama'a'. Arabic speakers do the same in English: i-sport, e-student, i-school.
facts.ar: تحلّ العربية ذلك بهمزة الوصل: كلمات مثل «اسْم» و«اسْتَمَعَ» تبدأ بحرف ساكن، والعربية لا تبدأ بساكن، فإذا بدأنا بها نطقنا همزة متحركة قبلها: «اِسْم». وفي وسط الكلام تسقط في النطق: «وَاسْتَمَعَ» تُقرأ «وَسْتَمَعَ». ويفعل متحدثو العربية الشيء نفسه مع الإنجليزية: إسبورت، إستيودنت، إسكول.

facts.en: English allows up to THREE consonants at the start: string, splash, spring. And up to four at the end: texts (k-s-t-s).
facts.ar: تسمح الإنجليزية بما يصل إلى ثلاثة أصوات صامتة في بداية الكلمة: string و splash و spring، وبما يصل إلى أربعة في آخرها: texts (k-s-t-s).

facts.en: Arabic speakers are not alone! Japanese speakers say 'su-to-rai-ku' for strike, and Spanish speakers say 'es-tudent'. Every brain fixes words to fit its own language's rules.
facts.ar: لستَ وحدك! يقول اليابانيون «سو-تو-راي-كو» بدل strike، ويقول الإسبان «إس-تيودنت». كل دماغ يعدّل الكلمات لتناسب قوانين لغته.

facts.en: ng is a real single sound made at the back of the mouth with air going through the nose. Arabic has something close to it: when ن without a vowel comes before ك (as in أنْكَر or منْك), the n moves back toward the k and sounds close to ng. In the tajweed rules of Quran recitation this is part of ikhfa' (الإخفاء): the noon is hidden, with a ghunna, before certain letters, including ك.
facts.ar: ng صوت واحد حقيقي يُصنع في مؤخرة الفم والهواء يخرج من الأنف. وفي العربية ما يقاربه: إذا جاءت النون الساكنة قبل الكاف (مثل: أنْكَر، منْك) انتقل مخرجها نحو مخرج الكاف فقاربت صوت ng. وفي أحكام التجويد لتلاوة القرآن الكريم يدخل هذا في الإخفاء: تُخفى النون الساكنة مع الغُنّة عند حروف معيّنة منها الكاف.

arabicBridge.point: Arabic needs a vowel between the two consonants, so the mouth breaks the cluster in the middle. In English, b and l touch: bl-.
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية تحتاج حركة بين الصامتين فيكسر الفم التجمّع من الوسط. أما في الإنجليزية فيلتصق b بـ l مباشرة.

arabicBridge.point: With s + consonant, Arabic speakers usually add the vowel BEFORE the s, much like the helping hamza (hamzat al-wasl) in اِسْم.
arabicBridge.pointAr: مع s وصوت صامت بعدها يضيف متحدث العربية الحركة قبل s عادة، كما في همزة الوصل في «اِسْم».

arabicBridge.english: Clusters in the middle and end: classroom, desk, hand
arabicBridge.point: Arabic allows two consonants at the end in pause (kalb, bint), so endings like desk and hand are easier than beginnings. Watch long middles: 'playground' must not become 'pilay-giround'.
arabicBridge.pointAr: تسمح العربية بساكنين في آخر الكلمة عند الوقف (كلْب، بنْت)، فالنهايات مثل desk و hand أسهل من البدايات. انتبه للكلمات الطويلة: playground لا تصبح «بِلاي-جِراوند».

arabicBridge.point: Arabic speakers often add a hard g: king-g, sing-g. In English the g is silent inside ng: the tongue stays at the back and the sound goes through the nose.
arabicBridge.pointAr: كثيراً ما يضيف متحدثو العربية صوت g منفصلاً في الآخر: king-g. في الإنجليزية يبقى اللسان في الخلف ويخرج الصوت من الأنف، ولا تُنطق g منفصلة.

commonErrors.why: Arabic does not start a syllable with two consonants, so a vowel slips between b and l. Clap test: black is ONE clap.
Sneaky vowel between p and l; also p can turn into b because Arabic has no p.
Hamzat al-wasl habit: a vowel before s + consonant. Start with a long hiss: sss-tudent.
Same as student: an extra vowel before s-clusters.
ng is one nose sound. The g is not pushed out at the end.
Sneaky vowel in L-blends: g-l and f-l must touch.

teacher: A rubber band or a picture of one (for stretch and snap)
Word cards: black, clap, flag, plum, slide, please, play, glasses, classroom, playground, student, school, sport, king, ring, sing, long, thing, think, thank you, pink
A 'Sneaky Vowel' character picture (a small ghost 'i' that sneaks into words)
student: Two paper cards: a green tick (clean) and a red ghost (sneaky vowel)

stages.name: Warm-up: Catch the Sneaky Vowel
stages.method: Listening hook with a character (the Sneaky Vowel ghost)
stages.purpose: Make the hidden problem visible: children hear the extra vowel when someone else says it.
teacherSays: Detectives, there is a thief in our class! It is the Sneaky Vowel. It hides inside words. Listen: bi-lack. Did you hear it? Bi-lack! Now: black. Clean!
When you hear the Sneaky Vowel, show the red ghost. When the word is clean, show the green tick.
Listen: pilease... please... flag... filag...
teacherSaysAr: في صفنا لصّ اسمه «الحركة المتسللة»، يختبئ داخل الكلمات.
إذا سمعت الحركة المتسللة ارفع الشبح الأحمر، وإذا كانت الكلمة نظيفة ارفع العلامة الخضراء.
studentsDo: Show the red ghost or the green tick for 6 quick words.
Say 'Gotcha!' when they catch the Sneaky Vowel.
tips: Exaggerate the wrong versions at first so everyone hears them; then make them more subtle.
The children are judging the TEACHER's voice first: this feels safe before they judge their own.

stages.name: Discovery: Digraph or Cluster?
stages.nameAr: اكتشاف: حرف مزدوج أم تجمّع صوامت؟
stages.method: Guided discovery with sound counting (link to Bonus Class 1)
stages.purpose: Tell apart two letters for one sound (sh) and two letters for two sounds (bl).
teacherSays: Remember Bonus Class 1? sh in fish: two letters, ONE sound. Now look at black: b-l. Say it slowly: b... l... ack. Can you hear the b AND the l? Yes! Two sounds.
When two consonant sounds stand side by side and we hear both, it is a cluster. Clusters are friends standing close; digraphs are friends who become one.
Detective question: is it ONE sound or TWO sounds?
teacherSaysAr: sh صوت واحد من حرفين. أما bl فصوتان نسمعهما معاً: هذا تجمّع صوامت.
الحرف المزدوج: صديقان أصبحا واحداً. التجمّع: صديقان يقفان متلاصقين.
studentsDo: Say each pair slowly and show 1 or 2 fingers.
Sort the letter pairs into two boxes: Digraph (1 sound) and Cluster (2 sounds).

exercise.instructions: One sound or two sounds? Write D for digraph or C for cluster.
exercise.instructionsAr: صوت واحد أم صوتان؟ اكتب D للحرف المزدوج و C لتجمّع الصوامت.

tips: ng is a digraph: two letters, one sound. Many children think they hear n + g; let them feel that the tongue does not move twice.
Keep the 'friends' image: it helps 8-year-olds remember the difference.

stages.name: Linguistics Corner and Arabic Bridge: Why the Sneaky Vowel Comes
stages.nameAr: ركن اللغويات وجسر العربية: لماذا تأتي الحركة المتسللة؟
stages.method: Contrastive analysis with Arabic syllable rules (hamzat al-wasl) + world languages
stages.purpose: Understand that the extra vowel comes from Arabic syllable rules, not from carelessness, and decide where it sneaks in.
teacherSays: Here is the secret. Every Arabic syllable starts with one consonant and a vowel: ka-ta-ba. Standard Arabic never starts a word with two consonants together.
When a word starts with sukun, Arabic adds a helper in front: اِسْم، اِسْتَمَعَ. That is hamzat al-wasl!
So your brain is clever: it adds i before student: i-student. Or it adds a vowel in the middle: bi-lack. Your brain is following Arabic rules.
And it's not only Arabic! Japanese speakers say su-to-rai-ku for strike. Spanish speakers say es-tudent.
English has different rules: up to three consonants at the start: string, splash. Our job: switch on English rules!
teacherSaysAr: المقطع العربي يبدأ بصوت صامت واحد ثم حركة، ولا تبدأ الكلمة العربية الفصيحة بساكن.
لذلك نضيف همزة وصل: اِسْم. ودماغك يفعل الشيء نفسه مع الإنجليزية لأنه ذكي ويتبع قوانين العربية.
studentsDo: Read اِسْم and اِسْتَمَعَ and notice the starting vowel.
Decide where the Sneaky Vowel hides in each wrong word: before (i-sport) or in the middle (bi-lack).
Say the correct word.

exercise.instructions: Where is the Sneaky Vowel: at the start or in the middle? Then say the clean word.
exercise.instructionsAr: أين الحركة المتسللة: في البداية أم في الوسط؟ ثم انطق الكلمة النظيفة.

tips: Say clearly: this is not a 'bad' habit, it is your Arabic grammar working. Children relax and improve faster.

Pattern for the teacher: s + p, t or k (sport, student, school) usually gets a vowel BEFORE it; most other clusters (including sl: su-lide) get a vowel IN THE MIDDLE. This is a tendency, not a law, and it varies by speaker and dialect.

stages.name: Rubber Band Blending: Stretch and Snap
stages.method: Multisensory blending (rubber band gesture) + add-a-sound word building
stages.purpose: Build clusters without a vowel by gluing a consonant onto a word the child already says well.
teacherSays: Take your invisible rubber band. Stretch it: b... lack. Now SNAP: black!
Trick number 1: start from the word you know. Say 'lack'. Now put b in front, close to lack, no space: b-lack, black!
Trick number 2 for s-words: start with a long snake sound: ssssss-tudent. The snake hisses straight into the t. No i before!
Trick number 3: say it slowly, then faster, faster, fastest!
teacherSaysAr: مُدّ المطاطة: b... lack ثم اتركها: black!
ابدأ بالكلمة التي تعرفها ثم ألصق الصوت الجديد في أولها بلا مسافة.
في كلمات s ابدأ بصوت ثعبان طويل sssss ولا تضع حركة قبله.
studentsDo: Stretch and snap with both hands for each word.
Say the base word, then add the first sound to make a cluster word.
Speed ladder: slow, faster, fastest for black, please, glasses, student.

exercise.instructions: Say the small word. Add the sound in front. Say the new word with NO sneaky vowel.
exercise.instructionsAr: انطق الكلمة الصغيرة، ثم أضف الصوت في أولها، وانطق الكلمة الجديدة بلا حركة متسللة.

tips: Add-a-sound works because the child already says 'lap' or 'top' perfectly; only the joint is new.
For p in play/please, remind children of the Level 1 tissue test: p has a puff of air.
S-clusters are a preview of Lesson 11; keep them light and fun.

stages.name: The King's Nose Sound: ng
stages.method: Articulation work (hold the nose test) + odd-one-out listening
stages.purpose: Say ng as one nasal sound with no hard g at the end, and hear ng vs n.
teacherSays: Say king. Now hold your nose and say nggg... it stops! The air goes through your nose. That is ng.
The back of your tongue goes up and stays there. No g kick at the end: king, not king-g.
Careful! In think, pink and thank you, we write n but we say ng too, and then a k: thi-ng-k.
Odd one out: ring, rin, ring... which is different?
teacherSaysAr: أمسك أنفك وقل nggg: يتوقف الصوت! لأن الهواء يخرج من الأنف.
لا تضف g قوية في آخر king.
studentsDo: Hold-the-nose test for n, m and ng (all stop).
Chant: 'The king can sing a long song. Ding dong!'
Listen: n or ng? Show 1 finger for n, 2 fingers for ng.

exercise.instructions: Does the word end in n or ng? Show 1 finger (n) or 2 fingers (ng).
exercise.instructionsAr: هل تنتهي الكلمة بـ n أم ng؟ أرِني إصبعاً واحداً لـ n أو إصبعين لـ ng.

tips: thin / thing and sun / sung are perfect minimal pairs that use Lesson 5 sounds.
In some English accents (for example in parts of northern England) a light g is heard; we teach the more common ng with no g.

stages.name: Clap Test and Cluster Chant
stages.method: Syllable clapping as self-check + choral chant + peer coaching
stages.purpose: Give children a self-check tool (beats) and lots of fluent practice with the class vocabulary.
teacherSays: Here is the detective's best tool: the Clap Test. black = 1 clap. If you clap twice, bi-lack, the Sneaky Vowel got in!
Let's clap: black (1), please (1), glasses (2), student (2), classroom (2), playground (2).
Now our chant. Slowly first, then fast!
Coach time: listen to your partner. If you hear the Sneaky Vowel, show the ghost and help them.
teacherSaysAr: اختبار التصفيق: black تصفيقة واحدة. إذا صفقت مرتين فقد دخلت الحركة المتسللة!
دور المدرّب: استمع لزميلك وساعده إذا سمعت الحركة المتسللة.
studentsDo: Clap the beats of each word and check that the cluster stays inside one clap.
Say the chant together: 'Black flag, clap clap! Please play, slide slide! Glasses in the classroom, students in the playground!'
Peer coaching: each child says 4 words; a partner checks with the green tick or red ghost.

exercise.instructions: Clap the word. How many beats? Keep the cluster inside one beat.
exercise.instructionsAr: صفّق للكلمة. كم مقطعاً فيها؟ أبقِ التجمّع داخل تصفيقة واحدة.

tips: The Clap Test is a tool children can use alone at home; make sure each child does it once by themselves.
Playground and eyebrow have clusters in the middle (gr, br): watch for 'pilay-giround'.
Bonus Class 4 builds on this clapping with syllables and stress.

stages.name: Production: My Classroom Tour
stages.method: Task-based speaking using lesson structures packed with clusters
stages.purpose: Use clusters in real sentences from Lessons 5-8, not only in single words.
teacherSays: Give us a tour of your classroom or room! Use 'There is...' and 'I have got...'.
Try to use 3 cluster words: black, glasses, please, play, flag, clock, student, classroom, playground.
Example: 'This is my classroom. There is a black clock. I have got glasses. Please play with me in the playground!'
teacherSaysAr: قدّم لنا جولة في صفك أو غرفتك واستخدم ثلاث كلمات فيها تجمّعات.
المستمعون: عدّوا الكلمات النظيفة بلا حركة متسللة!
studentsDo: Write 3 sentences with at least 3 cluster words.
Present the tour (30-40 seconds each) holding up real objects or pointing at the camera.
Listeners count the clean cluster words and give a star score.
tips: Correct only clusters in this stage; ignore other small errors so the focus stays clear.
Model the first tour yourself with one deliberate Sneaky Vowel for the children to catch.

stages.name: Exit Ticket, Did You Know? and Goodbye
stages.method: Formative check (listen and judge + say it) + curiosity close
stages.purpose: Check who hears the Sneaky Vowel and who can say the clusters cleanly.
teacherSays: Exit ticket: five words. Write G (green tick) if the word is clean, or R (red ghost) if something sneaky got in. Then each of you says one word for me.

Did you know? The English word 'strengths' has three consonant sounds at the start (s-t-r) and three at the end (ng-th-s)! Arabic speakers, Japanese speakers and Spanish speakers all find it a monster word.
Mission: teach your family the Clap Test with 'black' and 'please'.
teacherSaysAr: هل تعلم؟ كلمة strengths فيها ثلاثة أصوات صامتة في أولها وثلاثة في آخرها!
studentsDo: Judge 5 words (G or R).
Say one cluster word alone, cleanly.
tips: Note children who still add a vowel in L-blends; give them add-a-sound practice before Lesson 9 (R-blends).

exitTicket.instructions: Listen. Is the word clean (G, green tick) or did something sneaky get in (R, red ghost)?
exitTicket.instructionsAr: استمع: هل الكلمة نظيفة (G، العلامة الخضراء) أم دخلها صوت متسلل (R، الشبح الأحمر)؟

homework.en: Cluster Collector: find 6 things at home whose names start with a cluster (black bag, glass, clock, plate, slipper, plant...). Say each name 3 times without the Sneaky Vowel and do the Clap Test. Record yourself saying the cluster chant.
homework.ar: جامع التجمّعات: ابحث عن 6 أشياء في البيت تبدأ أسماؤها بتجمّع صوامت (black bag و glass و clock و plate و slipper و plant...). انطق كل اسم 3 مرات بلا حركة متسللة وطبّق اختبار التصفيق. سجّل صوتك وأنت تقول أنشودة التجمّعات.
tasks: Write 6 cluster words and underline the cluster.
Do the Clap Test for each word with a family member.
Say 'The king can sing a long song' three times with a clean ng.

support: Work only with L-blends (taught in Lesson 7) and leave S-clusters for later.
Use add-a-sound for every word: lack -> black, lay -> play.
Let the child whisper the first consonant, then say the rest aloud, then join them.
challenge: Three-consonant clusters: splash, string, spring, scream. Can you say them clean?
Find clusters at the end: hand, desk, lamp, milk, pink.
Explain hamzat al-wasl and the Sneaky Vowel to the group in English.

successCriteria: Explains digraph vs cluster with one example of each.
Says why Arabic speakers add a vowel (Standard Arabic syllables never start with two consonants).
Says black, please, flag and glasses with no added vowel (at least 3 of 4).
Hears the Sneaky Vowel in at least 4 of 5 exit-ticket items.
watchFor: p said as b in please and play

teacherNotes: The Sneaky Vowel is called epenthesis in linguistics. Arabic speakers often insert it before s + consonant (prothesis: i-sport) and between other consonants (anaptyxis: bi-lack). Where the vowel goes varies by speaker and dialect.
Never mock the error: frame it as the Arabic rule system doing its job. Children who understand the reason fix it faster.
R-blends (Lesson 9) and S-blends (Lesson 11) will reuse add-a-sound and the Clap Test; keep the red ghost card for those lessons.
Bonus Class 3 moves from consonants to vowels: long and short vowels, magic e and vowel teams.

Dialect note: Standard Arabic and Egyptian Arabic never start a word with two consonants. Some spoken dialects do (Levantine كْتير 'a lot', many North African words and some Gulf words), but learners from these regions still often add vowels to English clusters, because combinations like bl, sp and str are new to them.
